name: Maximilien Robespierre
role: French revolutionary; Jacobin leader and member of the Committee of Public Safety (1793-1794)
summary: Robespierre defended popular sovereignty, equal political rights and a limited, socially bound right of property, and he opposed the death penalty and the war of 1792 before leading the Terror in 1793-94. He opposed atheism and promoted a state cult of the Supreme Being. The sources searched cover his rights, constitutional and religious positions far better than his economic or social ones.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: He condemns the hereditary right of the dynasty and of nobles over vassals, and Art. XVIII admits all citizens to office with no title but virtue and talent.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: He makes relief of poverty a legal debt of the rich, set by law, not a matter of private charity.

church-by-bishops.rationale: In June 1790 he argued that bishops must be elected by the sovereign people and not by the clergy.

collective-defense.rationale: Art. XXXVI-XXXVII of his draft Declaration: whoever oppresses one nation is the enemy of all, and those who make war on a free people must be pursued by all.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Art. XIV-XV of his draft Declaration: law is the free expression of the people's will, the people are sovereign and the government is their work.

death-penalty.rationale: As leader of the Committee of Public Safety he presided over a Terror that ordered hundreds of executions of political enemies; his 1791 speech against capital punishment is left out because the record of 1793-94 answers it.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: Art. XI-XII make poor relief a social obligation and a debt of the rich to the poor.

democracy-best.rationale: He holds that the people are good and their delegates corruptible, and calls democracy the basis of the republic; he never weighs the case of voters choosing badly.

dynastic-succession.rationale: He denounces the dynasty's hereditary right as a right to oppress 25 million people.

elective-rulers.rationale: He calls the Capetian hereditary right a right to oppress, wants Louis condemned, and in Art. XIX gives every citizen an equal right to choose the people's mandataires.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: In 1794 he states that in revolution the people are led by reason and their enemies by terror, which he defines as prompt, severe, inflexible justice.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Art. III and XVII of his draft Declaration: rights belong equally to all men whatever their strength, and the law must be equal for all.

harm-principle.rationale: Art. V of his draft Declaration: law may forbid only what harms society; during the Terror his government went further.

job-guarantee.rationale: Art. XI says society must secure the subsistence of all by providing work or means of living to those unable to work; it does not name an employer of last resort.

limit-guns.rationale: In his speech on the National Guard he calls the right to be armed for personal defence and for the fatherland inalienable, for poor and rich alike.

mixed-constitution.rationale: He rejects the balance of powers and the tribunate and places power in the sovereign people (10 May 1793).

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: He demanded that Louis XVI be declared a traitor and die ('Louis must die so that the fatherland may live') and called kings slaves in revolt against humanity.

nation-first.rationale: Art. XXXV-XXXVI of his draft Declaration say men of all countries are brothers who should help each other, and that whoever oppresses one nation is the enemy of all.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Art. XXII requires citizens to obey magistrates carrying out the law, while Art. VI and XXIII deny the force of unjust law.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Art. XII of his draft Declaration calls relief for the poor a debt of the rich to the poor, set by law.

office-by-exam.rationale: Art. XVIII of his draft Declaration admits citizens to office with no title but the people's confidence.

person-over-state.rationale: Art. I of his draft Declaration makes the purpose of political association the maintenance of natural rights.

positive-liberty.rationale: Art. XXI says rights are illusory unless public officials are paid and working citizens can attend assemblies without risking their livelihood.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Art. XI-XII of his draft Declaration: society must provide subsistence for all, and relief for the poor is a debt of the rich.

property-franchise.rationale: He opposed the marc d'argent tax qualification for voting and argued that wealth cannot be the measure of merit.

property-fundamental.rationale: He calls property a social institution bounded like every other right, and says the Declaration protects it too much without defining its limits.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Art. VII-X of his draft Declaration: property is a right limited by respect for others' rights, may not harm their existence, and any possession or trade that does is illicit and immoral.

public-access-to-information.rationale: In the constitution speech he says the whole nation has the right to know its mandataires' conduct, wants deliberations in front of all the French, and Art. XXX gives the people the right to know all their operations.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: In November 1793 he says the Convention will keep freedom of worship and not persecute peaceful ministers, punishing only abuse to disturb order.

racial-franchise.rationale: In August 1791 he argued for equal civil and political rights for free men of colour in the colonies.

reason-over-faith.rationale: He argues that belief in a Supreme Being and immortality is popular and necessary to political morality, not mere private opinion.

recall-officials.rationale: Art. XVI of his draft Declaration: the people may at any time change their government and recall their mandataires.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Art. XXIII and XXV of his draft Declaration: acts beyond the law are void and may be repelled by force, and insurrection against a government that violates rights is a duty.

sacred-ruler.rationale: He treats kings as slaves in revolt against the sovereign of the earth, mankind, rather than as sacred.

second-chamber.rationale: In 1792 he describes the two-chamber system as the project of the court faction to raise one party over public liberty.

separate-church-state.rationale: His committee made the Cult of the Supreme Being the official national religion, replacing Christianity.

separated-powers.rationale: In his speech on the constitution of 10 May 1793 he calls the balance of powers a chimera or a scourge that ends in a league of rival powers against the people.

shared-human-nature.rationale: Art. III of his draft Declaration says equality of rights is established by nature and belongs to all men.

single-common-good.rationale: He contrasts the general will and the public interest with private interests, and wants only the general will consulted.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Art. XXX of his draft Declaration: no one may claim to be more inviolable than other citizens and officials' offences are to be punished severely.

spiritual-nature.rationale: In 1794 he speaks of tying man's passing life to God and immortality and defends the Supreme Being.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: In November 1793 he says a legislator would be a hundred times mad to adopt atheism as a system, and that atheism is aristocratic.

suppress-opposition.rationale: In 1793-94 he called for proscribing hostile papers and treated those who slander the government as enemies of the fatherland; this follows his earlier defence of press criticism, so it is not a firm answer.

universal-morality.rationale: He appeals to eternal laws of nature and justice and to natural, imprescriptible rights belonging to all men.

unjust-law-not-binding.rationale: Art. VI of his draft Declaration: a law that violates imprescriptible rights is unjust and tyrannical and 'is not a law'.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: In April 1793 he says the extreme disproportion of fortunes is the source of many evils and crimes.

notes: Over time: in 1791 he argued against capital punishment, and for freedom of the press; in 1793-94 he led a government that executed its political opponents and defended terror as justice. The 1793-94 record answers the death penalty. The progressive-tax article of his April 1793 draft was dropped from the version he later printed himself, so tax statements are left null. Themes searched: government and constitution, religion, property and welfare, rights and equality, war and foreign relations, colonies, press. Not found in the sources used: positions on gender, family, sexuality, trade, ecology, technology, immigration, and detailed economic policy, and the Maximum price controls and the law of 22 Prairial, which are left null.
